title: Handling customer complaint calls at a restaurant
seoTitle: Restaurant complaint calls: calm staff handling
description: Handle a restaurant complaint call with calm scripts, clear handoff steps, and a simple process that protects service and your team.
question: How should I handle a restaurant customer complaint phone call without making it worse?
answer: Start by listening, apologizing for the problem, and collecting the caller’s name, phone, order details, and what went wrong. Do not argue on the call; instead, give a clear next step, pass the complaint to the right staff member, and follow up with a fix or explanation. A phone host like ROAL can gather the basics and hand the call to staff with a summary when the issue needs a human.
summary: You’ll learn a simple complaint-call process, scripts, and handoff steps your team can use right away.
intro:
A restaurant customer complaint phone call should be handled calmly, fast, and with a clear next step. The goal is to listen, fix what you can, and move the problem to the right person without making the caller repeat themselves.

For independent restaurants, that matters because complaint calls often come in during rushes, when the counter is busy and the kitchen is moving. A simple script, a short handoff process, and a clear record of what happened can save time and protect the relationship with the guest. If you want a phone system that can gather the details first and pass tricky calls to staff, ROAL does that while still letting your team stay in control.

sections.h2: What should I say first on a complaint call?
sections.body:
Start with calm tone, then apology, then facts. Do not start by explaining why the customer is wrong.

A good opening sounds like this: "I’m sorry that happened. Let me get your name, order details, and the best phone number, and I’ll make sure the right person sees this right away."

Use this quick call flow:
1. Let the caller finish without interrupting.
2. Say sorry for the issue, even if you are still checking the facts.
3. Ask for the name, phone number, order time, and item(s) involved.
4. Repeat back the problem in one sentence.
5. Tell them what happens next.

A short checklist for the person answering:
- Stay calm and speak slowly.
- Do not blame the kitchen, driver, or guest on the call.
- Keep the caller on one topic at a time.
- Write down the complaint exactly as described.

If your shop uses [phone greeting templates](/tools/phone-greeting-templates), add one version for complaints so the team is not improvising under pressure.

sections.h2: What details do I need before I hand the call to staff?
sections.body:
For complaint calls, details matter. The more specific the note, the faster your manager can fix the issue without asking the guest to repeat everything.

Collect these items every time:
- Caller name
- Best callback number
- Order type: pickup or delivery
- Order time and date
- What was ordered
- What went wrong
- Whether the food is still with the caller
- Whether the caller wants a refund, remake, credit, or just a call back

You can turn that into a simple script line: "Can I get the name on the order, the phone number, and the item that had the problem?"

Here is a worked example you can swap for your own numbers:
- Say the guest ordered a $28 family meal at 6:40 p.m.
- They report that one item was missing.
- Your manager can check the kitchen ticket, the pickup shelf, and the phone log in a minute.

That kind of detail is especially useful when the call comes through [after-hours calls](/use-cases/after-hours) or during the dinner rush. ROAL can capture the basics and send a summary to staff when the issue needs a human answer.

sections.h2: How do I calm an upset guest without making promises I can’t keep?
sections.body:
You want to sound helpful, not defensive. At the same time, do not promise a refund, remake, or free item unless that is actually your policy.

A practical three-line response is:
1. "I’m sorry this happened."
2. "I’m getting the details now so the right person can review it."
3. "I’ll make sure staff sees this and follows up."

If the caller is heated, keep your voice even and avoid long explanations. Short sentences work best.

A few things to avoid:
- "That’s not possible."
- "You must have ordered the wrong item."
- "The kitchen said it was fine."
- "There’s nothing I can do."

Instead, try: "I hear you. Let me get the order details so we can look at it properly."

If the issue is about food quality, missing items, allergy-sensitive questions, or a manager request, route it to staff quickly. Those are exactly the kinds of calls ROAL hands off with a summary so the caller does not have to start over. For broader context on the system, see [How it works](/how-it-works).

sections.h2: When should a complaint stay with the phone host and when should it go to staff?
sections.body:
Not every complaint needs a manager on the line. Some calls just need information captured and passed along. Others need an immediate human response.

Use this simple split:

| Call type | Best next step |
|---|---|
| Missing item, wrong size, late pickup | Capture details and send to staff |
| Allergy-sensitive question | Hand to staff immediately |
| Caller wants the manager | Hand to staff immediately |
| General complaint about service | Capture details, then hand off |
| Question about hours or menu | Answer if you know it, or capture and route |

A good phone host should not guess on sensitive issues. ROAL is set up to hand allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, catering requests, and manager requests to staff with a summary.

A short internal rule helps a lot:
- Simple factual question: answer it if the menu, hours, or address are clear.
- Emotional or policy issue: hand it off.
- Safety issue: hand it off right away.

That keeps your team from arguing on the phone and gives the guest a faster path to the person who can solve the issue.

sections.h2: How can I train my staff to handle complaint calls the same way every time?
sections.body:
Consistency matters more than perfect wording. Your team does not need a long speech. They need a repeatable process.

Train the front counter, host stand, and manager on duty to use the same order:
1. Listen.
2. Apologize.
3. Gather facts.
4. Repeat the issue back.
5. Give a next step.

You can also write a one-page cheat sheet near the phone:
- What counts as a complaint
- Who gets the call
- What details to collect
- What can be promised at the counter
- Where to log the issue

Example script for staff: "I’m sorry about that. Let me get your name and the order time, and I’ll send this to the manager right now."

For multi-location operators, keep the process the same at every store. That way a caller gets the same answer whether they call the Jersey City shop or the Hoboken shop. If you run more than one location, [multiple locations](/use-cases/multi-location) can help you think through the workflow.

ROAL also helps with consistency because the host uses the same intake flow every time, and unanswered questions land in an inbox so the next call can be handled better.

sections.h2: How do call forwarding and handoff work when I’m too busy to answer?
sections.body:
If complaint calls come in while your line is slammed, forwarding can keep the call moving instead of dumping the guest into voicemail. You can forward all calls, or only unanswered and busy calls, depending on your phone setup.

Typical carrier or system options often look like this, but always confirm with your carrier and test it:
- On many landlines and some carriers, dial *72 then the forwarding number to forward all calls, and *73 to turn it off.
- On some GSM mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off.
- **61*number# often forwards unanswered calls.
- **67*number# often forwards busy calls.
- Verizon Wireless commonly uses *72, *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding.
- Business VoIP systems usually handle it in the web portal.

Here is the practical version for a restaurant owner:
1. Pick where complaint calls should land when you cannot answer.
2. Test the forwarding with a real call.
3. Make sure the person receiving the call knows what to say.
4. Turn forwarding off when you no longer need it.

ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and you can forward your existing number to it. That lets the host take the call first, gather the facts, and send the complaint to staff when needed. If you want carrier-specific reminders, use [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes).

sections.h2: What should I track after the call so the problem does not repeat?
sections.body:
A complaint call is useful only if someone sees the pattern later. Keep a simple log so you can spot repeat issues with the same item, the same time of day, or the same shift.

Track these fields in a notebook, spreadsheet, or your restaurant phone dashboard:
- Date and time
- Caller name and number
- Order number or order time
- Problem type
- Staff member who handled it
- Outcome
- Whether a remake, credit, or callback happened

A sample follow-up note might look like this:
- "Friday 7:15 p.m., pickup order, missing side, customer called back, manager reviewed ticket, remake offered."

That kind of record helps with two things:
- Training staff on the same mistake twice.
- Spotting menu items or rush-hour windows that cause more complaints.

If you use ROAL, you also get call history with transcripts and recordings, plus live tickets on the kitchen screen. That gives you a clean record of what the caller said and what your team saw.

takeaways: Answer complaint calls with apology, facts, and a clear next step.
Collect the caller’s name, number, order time, and exact issue before handing off.
Use one simple script so every staff member handles complaints the same way.
Forward busy or unanswered calls only after you test the setup with a real call.
Keep a complaint log so repeat problems are easier to spot and fix.

faq.q: What is the best way to answer a restaurant customer complaint phone call?
faq.a: Start by listening without interrupting, then apologize and collect the basic order details. Keep your response short and calm, and tell the caller what happens next. Do not argue on the phone or promise a fix you cannot make.

faq.q: Should the person answering the phone handle the complaint or transfer it right away?
faq.a: If it is a simple factual issue, the person answering can collect the details and pass it along. If the caller wants a manager, mentions an allergy, or is upset enough that policy matters, transfer it right away. The key is to avoid making the caller repeat the story twice.

faq.q: What details do I need from a customer who complains by phone?
faq.a: Get the caller’s name, phone number, order time, what was ordered, and what went wrong. Ask whether they want a callback, remake, credit, or just to report the issue. That gives staff enough context to review the order quickly.

faq.q: Can an AI phone host handle complaint calls for a restaurant?
faq.a: Yes, for the parts that are safe and routine. ROAL can collect the complaint details, take the caller’s name and number, and hand allergy-sensitive questions, manager requests, and other tricky calls to staff with a summary. It does not take card numbers over the phone, and it is not a substitute for a manager on sensitive issues.
